Urmila checked her email at the cyber cafe in Jhunjhunu every evening after her shift at the cooperative bank. By August she had seven rejections for junior data analyst roles, all polite, all vague.
Her friend Rekha, who ran the photocopy counter, said, "Ask them why."
So Urmila wrote to the three recruiters who had actually interviewed her: "Could you share one thing that would have made my application stronger?" Two replied. Both said the same thing in different words. Her portfolio showed neat charts, but never said what problem they solved or what a business should do next.
She sat with her three projects that weekend. The crop price chart became: "Which week should farmers in our district sell, and why?" The bank data became: "Why do small loan customers miss payments in March?" Each got a short recommendation at the end.
In October she sent the new portfolio out. Two interview calls came in the first week.

Still shaky. On the way back from coaching, a scooter hit a car at the Ring Road signal right in front of me. The rider was on the ground and not getting up.

The crash happened right outside the college gate in Kolkata: an auto-rickshaw tipped on its side after a bus clipped it. People shouted. Someone tried to pull the driver out by his arm.
Dilnaz felt her heart pounding. Then, oddly, the first-aid class from last term came back, like a list on a board. Safety first. Call for help. Don't move someone badly hurt unless there's danger. Say only what you know.
"Stop, don't pull him," she told the man. "Is anything leaking? Is there fire?" There wasn't. The driver was groaning, his leg bent wrong.
She turned to her friend Kunal. "Call 112. Tell them an auto overturned, one man injured, conscious, leg hurt." Kunal did.
When the ambulance crew arrived, one asked what happened. Dilnaz said, "I didn't see the moment it tipped. He's been awake the whole time. Nobody has moved him." The crew nodded and took over.

Saturday.
Something happened today and I want to get it down.
A motorbike and an auto collided at the market crossing. The rider was lying near the kerb, awake but bleeding from his arm. A crowd formed in seconds, maybe fifteen people, and everyone was just looking at each other.
I remembered a teacher saying crowds wait for someone to go first. So I went first. I pointed at a man in a blue shirt: "You, call 112. Tell them market crossing." I pointed at two boys: "You two, stand on the road and wave the traffic round." And an aunty with a shopping bag: "Can you get water and a cloth from the shop?" That was Uma aunty from our lane, it turned out.
Everyone moved. The ambulance came in ten minutes.
My hands only started shaking after. I'm telling Papa about it tonight.
Rashmi

The other driver, Kishore, got out red-faced. "You didn't even look!"
Leela felt her pulse jump, but kept her voice level. "Are you hurt? Anyone in your car?" He shook his head. She checked her passenger seat: her mother, just discharged, was fine, only startled.

"Nobody's hurt, and we've swapped details," Leela said. "But could you note it in your register?" The guard did. Kishore, calmer now, shook her hand.
